topics.title: 1.1.1 Discrete and Continuous Quantities
topics.learn: Everything around you that can be measured or counted is a quantity. Quantities come in two kinds. Discrete quantities are separate, countable items with specific values. You can count them one by one: 1, 2, 3 … There is nothing "in between". You cannot have 2.5 students in a classroom. Continuous quantities can take any value within a range. They flow smoothly without breaks. Water can be 30 °C, 30.5 °C, 30.51 °C, and so on — there is always another value in between.

topics.title: 1.1.2 Introduction to Digital Systems
topics.learn: A digital system is an electronic system that uses only two values: 0 and 1. These two values are called binary digits, or bits for short. Why only two values? Because it is easy for an electronic circuit to tell "voltage present" from "no voltage". Every number, letter, photo and song in a computer is finally stored as a long pattern of these bits. 0 represents OFF, LOW, or FALSE. 1 represents ON, HIGH, or TRUE.

topics.title: 1.1.3 Analog and Digital Signals
topics.learn: A signal is a changing voltage (or other quantity) that carries information. Analog signals are continuous signals that change smoothly over time, like a sine wave. Examples: the human voice, a traditional mercury thermometer. Digital signals have only two levels: HIGH (1) and LOW (0). They jump instantly between these values, which creates a square wave. Example: computer data.

topics.title: 1.1.4 Boolean Algebra
topics.learn: Boolean algebra was developed by the English mathematician George Boole. It is a kind of algebra that deals with only two values: TRUE (1) and FALSE (0). It is the foundation of digital electronics and computer programming — every if condition in a program is a small piece of Boolean algebra.

topics.title: 1.1.5 Boolean Operations
topics.learn: There are three basic Boolean operations. Every other operation can be made from them. 1. AND operation ( · ) — gives output 1 only when ALL inputs are 1. Expression: Y = A · B (often written just AB). 2. OR operation ( + ) — gives output 1 when ANY input is 1. Expression: Y = A + B. 3. NOT operation ( ' or ¯ ) — inverts (flips) the input. If the input is 1 the output is 0, and if the input is 0 the output is 1. It is a unary operation, meaning it works on only one operand. Expression: Y = A' (also written as A with a bar on top, A̅).

topics.title: 1.1.6 Truth Tables
topics.learn: A truth table shows all possible input combinations and the output for each one, for a logic gate or a circuit. It is the "complete record" of how the circuit behaves. How to create a truth table: Count the number of inputs (n). Calculate total rows = 2n. List all input combinations in binary counting order (0, 1, 2, 3 … in binary). Calculate the output for each combination.

topics.title: 1.1.7 Logic Gates (Basic Gates: AND, OR, NOT)
topics.learn: Logic gates are electronic circuits that perform Boolean operations. They take one or more input bits and produce one output bit. They are the building blocks of all digital systems — a processor contains billions of them. The three basic gates match the three basic operations: the AND gate, the OR gate and the NOT gate (also called an inverter).

topics.title: 1.1.7 Universal Logic Gates (NAND and NOR)
topics.learn: NAND means "NOT AND": it is an AND gate followed by a NOT. NOR means "NOT OR": an OR gate followed by a NOT. On the symbol, the NOT is shown as a small bubble at the output. NAND and NOR are called universal gates because any logic circuit in the world can be built using only NAND gates (or only NOR gates). Factories like this: they can mass-produce one type of chip and build everything from it.

topics.learn: XOR (Exclusive OR) gives output 1 when the inputs are different. Expression: Y = A ⊕ B. In terms of basic operations, A ⊕ B = A'B + AB'. XNOR (Exclusive NOR) is XOR followed by NOT. It gives output 1 when the inputs are the same. Expression: Y = (A ⊕ B)' = A'B' + AB. The XOR symbol is an OR symbol with an extra curved line at the input side. XNOR adds a bubble at the output.

topics.title: 1.1.8 – 1.1.10 Logic Expressions, Minterms and Maxterms
topics.learn: A logic expression (Boolean expression) combines variables with operations, for example Y = A + B'·C. To evaluate it correctly you must follow the order of precedence, just like BODMAS in maths: Sometimes you are given a truth table and must find the expression. There are two standard ways. Minterm (used in SOP — Sum of Products): a product (AND) of all the variables, written for a row whose output is 1. A variable is complemented (A') if its value is 0, and uncomplemented (A) if its value is 1. OR-ing all the minterms gives the SOP expression. Maxterm (used in POS — Product of Sums): a sum (OR) of all the variables, written for a row whose output is 0. A variable is complemented (A') if its value is 1, and uncomplemented (A) if its value is 0. AND-ing all the maxterms gives the POS expression.

topics.title: 1.1.11 Logic Diagrams
topics.learn: A logic diagram shows how logic gates are connected to create a circuit. It is a "picture" of a Boolean expression. To draw one, use the order of precedence: the operation with the highest priority is drawn first (nearest the inputs), and the last operation is the gate that gives the final output.

topics.title: 1.1.13 Karnaugh Maps (K-Maps)
topics.learn: A Karnaugh map (K-map) is a graphical tool used to simplify Boolean expressions. It is a grid of cells — one cell for each row of the truth table. The cells are arranged so that neighbouring (adjacent) cells differ by only ONE bit. This ordering is called Gray code. You write the output (1 or 0) of each row into its cell, then group the 1s in rectangles of size 1, 2, 4 or 8 (powers of 2). Each group becomes one simple term. This simplifies the equation without long algebra. Grouping rules Group only 1s. Groups must be rectangles of size 1, 2, 4 or 8 — never 3, 5 or 6. Make groups as large as possible. Bigger groups give simpler terms. Use as few groups as possible, but every 1 must be in at least one group. Overlapping is allowed — a 1 may be used in more than one group. Wrapping around the edges is allowed: a cell in the far-left column is adjacent to the cell in the far-right column (BC = 00 is next to BC = 10). To read a group: variables that change (0 to 1) inside the group are eliminated. Variables that stay the same are kept — plain if they stay 1, complemented if they stay 0.

topics.title: LogiSim Evolution: Simulation Tool
topics.learn: LogiSim Evolution is a free graphical tool for designing and simulating logic circuits. "Simulating" means the computer pretends to be the real circuit: you can switch inputs on and off and watch the output change. It lets you see the truth tables and Boolean expressions you learn in theory.

topics.title: 1.2.1 – 1.2.3 Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)
topics.learn: The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is a structured process that guides software development from beginning to end. It ensures clear goals, better planning, risk reduction and high quality. Without it, teams forget features, go over budget and deliver buggy software. SDLC has 6 phases:

topics.title: 1.2.4 The Agile Model
topics.learn: The Agile model is an iterative approach: the software is built in small, repeated cycles called sprints (usually 2–4 weeks long). Each sprint plans, builds and tests a small part of the software, and then shows it to the customer. Customer feedback is gathered continuously and used in the next sprint.

topics.title: 1.2.5 – 1.2.7 Waterfall vs Agile: Comparison and Case Studies
topics.learn: Both models follow the same SDLC phases. The difference is how they move through them: Waterfall goes through each phase once, in a straight line; Agile goes through all phases many times, in small loops.

topics.title: 1.3.1 – 1.3.4 Communication Models and the OSI 7-Layer Model
topics.learn: A communication model explains how data travels from one device to another through a network. Because sending data is complicated, the job is split into layers; each layer does one part of the job and passes the data to the next layer. The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) model was developed by ISO (International Organization for Standardization) in 1984. It divides communication into 7 layers. When you send data, it goes down the layers on your device (7 → 1), travels as bits over the cable or air, and goes up the layers on the receiving device (1 → 7).

topics.title: 2.1 Computational Thinking
topics.learn: Computational Thinking (CT) is a systematic approach to solving problems. "Systematic" means you follow a fixed, organised method instead of guessing. CT involves four activities: CT is not "thinking like a computer". It is thinking in a way that lets you describe a solution so clearly that a computer (or another person) could carry it out. Decomposition — breaking a big problem down into smaller parts. Pattern recognition — identifying things that repeat or follow a rule. Abstraction — hiding (ignoring) details that do not matter. Algorithms — developing clear step-by-step instructions to solve the problem. Did you know? Pseudocode is a human-readable representation of an algorithm using plain English and structured programming keywords. It is the bridge between human logic and machine code. You will study it in detail in section 2.2.2.

topics.title: 2.2 Algorithm
topics.learn: An algorithm is a step-by-step logical procedure used to solve a problem. It is conceptual in nature (it is an idea, a plan) and completely independent of any programming language. The same algorithm can be written later in Python, C++ or Java. A good algorithm has: Input — the data it starts with. Clear steps — each step has only one meaning. A definite end — it must finish after a limited number of steps. Output — the result it produces.

topics.title: 2.2.2 Algorithm vs Pseudocode
topics.learn: Both algorithms and pseudocode are used in problem-solving, but they serve different purposes in the design phase. The algorithm says what must be done. The pseudocode shows how it could be implemented, using programming-like keywords such as IF, FOR and WHILE, but it still cannot be run on a computer.
topics.urdu: الگورتھم بتاتا ہے کہ کیا کرنا ہے، جبکہ سوڈو کوڈ (Pseudocode) بتاتا ہے کہ اسے کیسے کیا جا سکتا ہے۔ الگورتھم سادہ مرحلوں میں لکھا جاتا ہے اور ہر کوئی اسے سمجھ سکتا ہے۔ سوڈو کوڈ میں IF، FOR اور WHILE جیسے الفاظ استعمال ہوتے ہیں اور یہ زیادہ تر پروگرامرز کے لیے ہوتا ہے، لیکن اسے کمپیوٹر پر چلایا نہیں جا سکتا۔

Sketchnote کھولو اور algorithm والا حصہ انگلی سے دباؤ۔ میں یہ line پڑھ کر نہیں گزر رہی۔ Line یہ کہتی ہے: الگورتھم بتاتا ہے کہ کیا کرنا ہے، Pseudocode بتاتا ہے کہ اسے کیسے کیا جا سکتا ہے۔۔ Intermediate student کے لیے مطلب یہ ہے کہ نام لکھ دینا کافی نہیں۔ تمہیں بتانا ہے کہ یہ rule کب کام کرتا ہے اور کب نہیں کرتا۔ algorithm English میں رہے گا۔ اس کا جوڑ pseudocode سے ہے۔ اگر examiner پوچھے کہ فرق کیا ہے، تو یوں جواب دو: الگورتھم سادہ مرحلوں میں لکھا جاتا ہے اور ہر کوئی اسے سمجھ سکتا ہے۔۔ اب دس سیکنڈ رکو۔ اپنی کاپی بند کرو اور algorithm کی ایک example بولو۔ پھر sketchnote کھول کر دیکھو کہ تمہاری example اسی rule پر کھڑی ہے یا نہیں۔ Minute 2. اب pseudocode کو غلط تعریف سے الگ کرو۔ لوگ اکثر pseudocode اور algorithm کو ایک ہی چیز سمجھ لیتے ہیں۔ Sketchnote کہتی ہے: الگورتھم سادہ مرحلوں میں لکھا جاتا ہے اور ہر کوئی اسے سمجھ سکتا ہے۔۔ اس کا مطلب یہ نہیں کہ سوڈو کوڈ میں IF، FOR اور WHILE جیسے الفاظ استعمال ہوتے ہیں اور یہ زیادہ تر پروگرامرز کے لیے ہوتا ہے، لیکن اسے کمپیوٹر پر چلایا نہیں جا سکتا۔۔ ایک mark تب ملتا ہے جب تم pseudocode کا نام اور ایک سچی بات لکھو۔ تین marks تب ملتے ہیں جب نام کے بعد reason ہو، اور reason الگورتھم سادہ مرحلوں میں لکھا جاتا ہے اور ہر کوئی اسے سمجھ سکتا ہے۔ سے آئے۔ پانچ marks کے لیے وہی reason، پھر ایک local example، پھر diagram یا table کا اشارہ۔ Local example school، phone، JazzCash، یا load-shedding سے دو، مگر term English میں لکھو۔ اگر example algorithm کے rule پر چلی جائے تو جواب غلط ہے۔ دوبارہ چیک کرو۔ Minute 3. Diagram اور table کی طرف آؤ، paragraph دوبارہ نہ پڑھو۔ Picture یا row یہ بتا رہی ہے: سوڈو کوڈ میں IF، FOR اور WHILE جیسے الفاظ استعمال ہوتے ہیں اور یہ زیادہ تر پروگرامرز کے لیے ہوتا ہے، لیکن اسے کمپیوٹر پر چلایا نہیں جا سکتا۔۔ Intermediate paper میں figure تب نمبر دیتی ہے جب labels English میں ہوں اور تم بتاؤ کہ arrow یا column کیا فرق دکھا رہا ہے۔ algorithm والی طرف ایک حقیقت رکھو، pseudocode والی طرف دوسری۔ دوسری حقیقت یہ ہے: Both algorithms and pseudocode are used in problem-solving, but they serve different purposes in the design phase.۔ اب ایک row زور سے بول دو، پھر آنکھ بند کرکے وہی row دوبارہ بول دو۔ جو لفظ بھولے، وہی exam میں کٹتا ہے۔ اسے ابھی sketchnote پر نشان لگاو۔ Minute 4. Example کو آہستہ چلاؤ، جیسے تم کسی دوست کو سمجھا رہے ہو۔ شروع کی بات یہ ہے: Both algorithms and pseudocode are used in problem-solving, but they serve different purposes in the design phase.۔ اگلا قدم خود نکالو، میں answer ابھی نہیں دے رہی۔ سوچنے کے لیے رک جاؤ۔ اب جواب ملا کر دیکھو: The algorithm says what must be done.۔ اگر تمہارا قدم اس سے مختلف ہے تو پوچھو کہ input وہی ہے یا تم نے pseudocode کا rule بدل دیا۔ Code ہو تو syntax مت رٹو۔ ہر line کا مقصد بولو: data اندر کیا آیا، decision کہاں ہوا، result کیا بدلا۔ pseudocode اور algorithm دونوں English میں رہیں، وضاحت Urdu میں دو۔ Minute 5. غلطی کا کلینک۔ Intermediate student algorithm کی definition لکھ کر رک جاتا ہے۔ Paper یہ نہیں پوچھتا کہ تمہیں sentence یاد ہے۔ Paper پوچھتا ہے کہ sentence اس case پر لگتا ہے یا نہیں۔ غلط اطلاق تب ہوتا ہے جب تم The algorithm says what must be done. کو The pseudocode shows how it could be implemented, using programming-like keywords such as IF, FOR and WHILE, but it still cannot be run on a computer. پر چسپاں کر دو۔ صحیح چیک یہ ہے: پہلے بتائو کہ case count ہے یا measure، name ہے یا process، input ہے یا output۔ پھر algorithm رکھو۔ اگر case pseudocode کا ہے تو پہلا نام کاٹ دو۔ جواب کے آخر میں ایک لائن لکھو: اس لیے یہ algorithm ہے، کیونکہ The algorithm says what must be done.۔ Minute 6. تین marks کا جواب ابھی بناؤ، کتاب بند رکھ کر۔ پہلی لائن: pseudocode وہ ہے جس کے بارے میں sketchnote کہتی ہے، The pseudocode shows how it could be implemented, using programming-like keywords such as IF, FOR and WHILE, but it still cannot be run on a computer.۔ دوسری لائن: یہ algorithm نہیں، کیونکہ The same problem written both ways: print whether a number is even or odd.۔ تیسری لائن: میری example۔ example میں نام English، صورتحال اپنی۔ اب کتاب کھولو اور تینوں لائنیں sketchnote سے ملاؤ۔ جو لائن board پر نہیں بنتی، اسے کاٹ دو۔ جو لائن بنتی ہے، اسے دوبارہ آہستہ بولو تاکہ زبان پر بیٹھ جائے۔ یہ reading نہیں۔ یہ وہ جواب ہے جو تم ہال میں لکھو گے۔ Minute 7. topics.title: 2.3.1 Decomposition
topics.learn: Decomposition is a problem-solving technique in which a complex task or system is broken down into smaller, manageable parts. By dividing a big problem into simpler steps, it becomes easier to understand, develop and solve. Each small part is called a sub-task (or sub-problem). You solve each sub-task separately, then join the solutions to solve the whole problem.

topics.learn: Pattern recognition is the process of identifying regularities, repetitions or rules in data. It helps in reducing the overall complexity of an algorithm and forms the foundation of concepts such as loops. How it works — ask yourself three questions: What is repeating? What changes in a predictable way? Can I generalise this (write one rule that works for every case)?

topics.title: 2.3.3 Abstraction
topics.learn: Abstraction means hiding unnecessary features and focusing only on the essential ones needed to solve a problem. It reduces complexity by ignoring what is not important (the noise). When you apply abstraction you sort details into three groups: Necessary steps — the core logic that never changes. Changes based on the situation — these become variables (inputs) in the algorithm. Abstraction items (noise) — details you can ignore completely.

topics.title: 2.4 Sorting and Searching Algorithms
topics.learn: Sorting and searching are both fundamental techniques of computer science. They work on lists of the same data type (for example, a list of all integers or a list of all names).

topics.title: 2.4.1 Sorting Algorithms: Bubble Sort
topics.learn: Bubble Sort is an elementary sorting algorithm that works by repeatedly comparing adjacent (side-by-side) elements and swapping them if they are in the wrong order. In each pass, the largest remaining value "bubbles up" to the end of the list, like an air bubble rising to the top of water. So after pass 1 the largest value is in the last place, after pass 2 the second largest is in second-last place, and so on. A list of N items needs N − 1 passes, and pass K makes N − K comparisons.

topics.title: 2.4.1 Sorting Algorithms: Selection Sort
topics.learn: Selection Sort is a simple sorting algorithm that works by repeatedly selecting the smallest element from the unsorted portion of the list and moving it to its correct position at the front. Think of it as filling seats from the front: first find who belongs in position 1, then position 2, and so on. In the textbook version, the element at position K is compared with every element after it; whenever a smaller one is found, the two are swapped. So at the end of pass K, the K-th smallest value sits in position K.

topics.learn: Linear Search, also known as sequential search, works by examining each element in the list one by one, from the start, until the target is found (or the list ends). It works on both sorted and unsorted data. A flag variable (here ValueFound) starts at 0 and becomes 1 when the item is found. After the loop, the flag tells us whether to print the item or "Not Found".

topics.title: 2.4.2 Searching Algorithms: Binary Search
topics.learn: Binary Search is a highly efficient search algorithm that works by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. Crucial limitation: it only works on a SORTED list. Three variables mark the part of the list still being searched: At each step compare the item with DATA[MID]: If BEG becomes greater than END, the part is empty and the item is not in the list. BEG (low) — first position of the current part. END (high) — last position of the current part. MID = INT((BEG + END) / 2) — the middle position. INT means "drop the decimal part". Equal → found, stop. Item < DATA[MID] → the item can only be in the left half: set END = MID − 1. Item > DATA[MID] → the item can only be in the right half: set BEG = MID + 1.

topics.learn: Before choosing an algorithm, ask three questions: Simple decision guide: What is the input size? (10 items or 10 million?) Is the data sorted? Do we need speed or memory efficiency? topics.title: 3.1 Programming
topics.learn: Computers are "dumb" machines. They are very fast, but they cannot think or do anything on their own. They need exact, step-by-step instructions. A set of instructions given to a computer is called a program. The language used to write these instructions is called a programming language. Writing programs is called programming, and the person who writes them is a programmer.

topics.title: 3.1.1 Programming Language Types
topics.learn: Programming languages are classified into three main types, depending on how close they are to the computer's own language (binary 0s and 1s) or to human language.

topics.title: 3.2 Career Growth with Python
topics.learn: Python is one of the most in-demand languages in the world. Learning it opens many career paths: Software Development: build desktop and web applications. Data Science and Data Analysis: analyse data, create reports and make predictions. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: develop intelligent systems, chatbots and recommendation algorithms (like "videos you may like"). Web Development: use frameworks such as Django and Flask to build websites. Automation and Scripting: automate repetitive office or lab tasks (renaming 500 files, filling spreadsheets). Cybersecurity and Networking: write security tools and analyse network data.

topics.title: 3.3 Integrated Development Environment (IDE)
topics.learn: An IDE (Integrated Development Environment) is a software tool that helps programmers write, run and manage code in one place. It is a complete workspace for programming. "Integrated" means many tools are joined together in one window. Key features of an IDE: Code Editor: where you write and edit code. Syntax Highlighting: colours different parts of the code (keywords, strings, numbers) to make it easier to read. Auto-completion: suggests code while you type (type pri and it offers print). Run/Execute Tool: runs the program with one click. Debugger: helps you find and fix errors, for example by pausing the program at a chosen line.

topics.title: 3.3.1 Visual Studio Code (VS Code)
topics.learn: VS Code is a free, lightweight and powerful code editor made by Microsoft and widely used for Python. By default it is not a full IDE, but it becomes one when you install extensions (add-ons), such as the Python extension by Microsoft.
topics.urdu: وی ایس کوڈ (VS Code) ایک مفت اور ہلکا پھلکا کوڈ ایڈیٹر ہے۔ یہ اپنے آپ میں مکمل آئی ڈی ای نہیں، لیکن ایکسٹینشنز (Extensions) لگانے سے آئی ڈی ای بن جاتا ہے۔ اس کے اہم حصے مینو بار، سائیڈ بار، ایکسپلورر، سرچ، سورس کنٹرول، رن اینڈ ڈیبگ اور ایکسٹینشنز ہیں۔

topics.title: 3.4 Fundamentals of Python Programming
topics.learn: The basic structure of a Python program is simple and clear. A program takes data, processes it using statements, and finally shows output. Python runs the statements top to bottom, one after another (sequentially). A statement is one complete instruction, usually written on one line, such as print("Hi") or x = 5. 1. Comments (#) — Comments are notes written in the code for humans. They start with the # symbol. The Python interpreter completely ignores them. Use them to explain what your code does. 2. Indentation (spaces) — C++ and Java use curly brackets { } to mark a block of code (a group of statements that belong together). Python instead uses indentation: spaces at the beginning of a line. Indentation is mandatory in Python. The standard is 4 spaces (or 1 tab).

topics.title: 3.4.1 Variables
topics.learn: A variable is a named space in computer memory used to store data. Think of it as a labelled container (a box with a name written on it). You put a value in it with the assignment operator =, which means "store", not "equals". In Python you do not need to declare the type of a variable. Python figures it out automatically from the value. This is called dynamic typing: the same variable can later hold a different type. Rules for naming variables: Can contain letters, numbers and underscores (_) only — no spaces or symbols like -, @, $. Must start with a letter or underscore, NOT a number (1name is invalid). Are case-sensitive: age and Age are two completely different variables. Cannot be a Python keyword (a reserved word such as if, for, while, else, True).

topics.title: 3.4.2 Input and Output Handling
topics.learn: Output — the print() function. A function is a named, ready-made piece of code that does a job when you call it with brackets. print() displays information on the screen. Input — the input() function. It shows a message (a prompt), pauses the program and waits for the user to type something and press Enter. Whatever the user types is always a string by default. Type casting means converting a value from one type to another: int() converts to an integer, float() to a decimal number, str() to a string. Items separated by commas are printed with one space between them. An f-string (a string with f before the quote) lets you put variables directly inside { }. It is the fastest and most readable way to format output.

topics.learn: An operand is the value or variable being worked on. An operator is the symbol that performs the action. Together they form an expression, which Python evaluates to a single value. In 10 + 20: 10 is an operand, + is the operator, 20 is an operand, and the result is 30. 1. Arithmetic operators do maths:

topics.title: 3.4.3 Bitwise Operators
topics.learn: 6. Bitwise operators treat numbers as binary digits (bits: 0s and 1s) and work on them bit by bit, column by column. Think of each bit as a switch that is ON (1) or OFF (0). Python's bin() function shows the binary form of a number (it starts with 0b). AND (&) — gives 1 only if both bits are 1, otherwise 0. OR (|) — gives 1 if at least one bit is 1. XOR (^) — gives 1 if the bits are different, 0 if they are the same. NOT (~) — inverts all bits (0 → 1, 1 → 0). In Python the result is the number made negative, minus 1: ~x = -(x + 1). So ~10 gives -11. Left shift (<<) — moves bits left and adds 0s on the right. Each shift multiplies by 2. Right shift (>>) — moves bits right and removes the rightmost bits. Each shift divides by 2 (floor division).

topics.title: 3.5 Control Structures
topics.learn: Control structures decide the order in which statements are executed in a program (the "flow of control"). Almost every program is built from just three basic structures: Sequence — do the steps one after another, top to bottom. Selection — choose a path depending on a condition (if, else). Repetition — repeat steps (loops: for, while).

topics.title: 3.5.1 Sequence
topics.learn: Sequence means statements are executed one after another, strictly from top to bottom, in the exact order they are written. This is the default behaviour of Python. No statement is skipped or repeated.

topics.title: 3.5.2 Selection Statements: if and if-else
topics.learn: Selection changes the flow of a program based on a condition — an expression that is either True or False. It helps a program respond intelligently to different situations. 1. The if statement executes a block of code only if the condition is True. If the condition is False, the block is completely skipped. 2. The if-else statement provides two paths: if the condition is true, do this; else (otherwise), do that. Exactly one of the two blocks always runs.

topics.title: 3.5.2 Selection Statements: if-elif-else and Nested if
topics.learn: 3. The if-elif-else statement handles many conditions. (elif is short for "else if".) Python checks the conditions from top to bottom. As soon as it finds a True condition, it runs that block and ignores all the rest. If none is True, the else block runs. 4. Nested if is an if inside another if. It is used when a decision needs to pass several levels of checks: the inner check happens only if the outer check passed.

topics.learn: A repetition statement (loop) lets a block of code run again and again. This greatly reduces the need to write the same code many times. Each single run of the loop body is called an iteration. 1. The for loop is used when the exact number of iterations is known. It takes each value from a sequence one by one and stores it in the loop variable (e.g. i). The range() function generates the sequence of numbers for the loop:

topics.title: 3.5.3 The while Loop, break and continue
topics.learn: 2. The while loop repeats a block of code as long as a condition remains True. It is used when the exact number of iterations is not known in advance (for example, "keep asking until the password is correct"). A while loop needs three parts: (1) initialise a variable before the loop, (2) test the condition, (3) update the variable inside the loop. If you forget the update, the condition never becomes False and the loop never stops — an infinite loop. Loop control statements change the normal flow of a loop: break — exits (stops) the loop entirely and immediately. continue — skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one.

topics.title: 3.5.3 Nested Loops and for vs while
topics.learn: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. The inner loop runs completely, from start to finish, for every single iteration of the outer loop. If the outer loop runs 2 times and the inner loop runs 3 times, the inner body runs 2 × 3 = 6 times.

topics.title: Practical Activity: Shopping Bill Calculator
topics.learn: This program combines all three control structures: sequence (steps in order), selection (checking "done", checking the price, checking for a discount) and repetition (a while loop that keeps adding items). It uses a flag — a Boolean variable (shopping) that controls when the loop stops. item.lower() converts the text to lowercase so that "done", "Done" and "DONE" all work.

topics.title: 3.6 Libraries in Python
topics.learn: A library (also called a module) is a collection of pre-written code that offers ready-made functions. Instead of writing a square-root algorithm from scratch, you import math and call math.sqrt(). Libraries save time, reduce bugs and let you stand on other programmers' work. There are five common ways to import a library. Method 3 (import only what you need) is the best habit: it is clearer and uses less memory than from math import *.

topics.title: 3.6.1 Built-in Libraries
topics.learn: Built-in libraries come pre-installed with Python. You only import them; you do not run pip. Three that every Class XI student must know are math, random and datetime.

topics.title: 3.6.2 Third-Party Libraries
topics.learn: Third-party libraries are written by the community. They are not bundled with Python, so you install them from a terminal with pip install library_name and then import them as usual.
topics.urdu: تھرڈ پارٹی لائبریریاں پائتھن کے ساتھ نہیں آتیں، انہیں pip install سے انسٹال کیا جاتا ہے۔ نمپائی، پینڈاز، میٹپلاٹ لیب اور ٹینسر فلو اسی قسم کی ہیں۔
topics.spokenUrdu: Minute 1. Sketchnote کھولو اور Third-party libraries والا حصہ انگلی سے دباؤ۔ میں یہ line پڑھ کر نہیں گزر رہی۔ Line یہ کہتی ہے: تھرڈ پارٹی لائبریریاں پائتھن کے ساتھ نہیں آتیں، انہیں pip install سے انسٹال کیا جاتا ہے۔۔ Intermediate student کے لیے مطلب یہ ہے کہ نام لکھ دینا کافی نہیں۔ تمہیں بتانا ہے کہ یہ rule کب کام کرتا ہے اور کب نہیں کرتا۔ Third-party libraries English میں رہے گا۔ اس کا جوڑ not سے ہے۔ اگر examiner پوچھے کہ فرق کیا ہے، تو یوں جواب دو: نمپائی، پینڈاز، میٹپلاٹ لیب اور ٹینسر فلو اسی قسم کی ہیں۔۔ اب دس سیکنڈ رکو۔ اپنی کاپی بند کرو اور Third-party libraries کی ایک example بولو۔ پھر sketchnote کھول کر دیکھو کہ تمہاری example اسی rule پر کھڑی ہے یا نہیں۔ Minute 2. اب not کو غلط تعریف سے الگ کرو۔ لوگ اکثر not اور Third-party libraries کو ایک ہی چیز سمجھ لیتے ہیں۔ Sketchnote کہتی ہے: نمپائی، پینڈاز، میٹپلاٹ لیب اور ٹینسر فلو اسی قسم کی ہیں۔۔ اس کا مطلب یہ نہیں کہ Third-party libraries are written by the community.۔ ایک mark تب ملتا ہے جب تم not کا نام اور ایک سچی بات لکھو۔ تین marks تب ملتے ہیں جب نام کے بعد reason ہو، اور reason نمپائی، پینڈاز، میٹپلاٹ لیب اور ٹینسر فلو اسی قسم کی ہیں۔ سے آئے۔ پانچ marks کے لیے وہی reason، پھر ایک local example، پھر diagram یا table کا اشارہ۔ Local example school، phone، JazzCash، یا load-shedding سے دو، مگر term English میں لکھو۔ اگر example Third-party libraries کے rule پر چلی جائے تو جواب غلط ہے۔ دوبارہ چیک کرو۔ Minute 3. Diagram اور table کی طرف آؤ، paragraph دوبارہ نہ پڑھو۔ Picture یا row یہ بتا رہی ہے: Third-party libraries are written by the community.۔ Intermediate paper میں figure تب نمبر دیتی ہے جب labels English میں ہوں اور تم بتاؤ کہ arrow یا column کیا فرق دکھا رہا ہے۔ Third-party libraries والی طرف ایک حقیقت رکھو، not والی طرف دوسری۔ دوسری حقیقت یہ ہے: They are not bundled with Python, so you install them from a terminal with pip install library_name and then import them as usual.۔ اب ایک row زور سے بول دو، پھر آنکھ بند کرکے وہی row دوبارہ بول دو۔ جو لفظ بھولے، وہی exam میں کٹتا ہے۔ اسے ابھی sketchnote پر نشان لگاو۔ Minute 4. topics.title: 3.7 Debugging Code in Python
topics.learn: Debugging is the process of identifying, tracing and fixing bugs so a program works correctly. Every program you write will have bugs. The skill is not "never make a mistake"; it is "find the mistake quickly". Python errors fall into three families:

topics.title: 4.1.1 Data, Information and Database
topics.learn: Data are unprocessed facts, figures or observations. They can be quantitative (numbers: 80, 75, 90) or qualitative (descriptions: the colours of cars in a parking lot). Data on its own is not very useful — a list of marks does not yet tell you whether the class is strong. When you organise, process and interpret data, it becomes information. Information has meaning and supports a decision. Example: “The class average is 80%, so we can move to the next chapter.” A database is an organised collection of related data, stored in a structured way so it can be accessed, managed and updated easily. Paper registers and loose files make searching painful; a database is built for search, update and sharing.

topics.title: 4.1.2 Database Management System (DBMS)
topics.learn: A DBMS is software that lets you create, manage and interact with databases. It sits between the user and the stored files. You never edit raw data files by hand — you talk to the DBMS (Access, MySQL, Oracle, SQLite) and it handles storage, security and consistency. Advantages you must be able to list: Less redundancy. The department name is stored once, not in every student row. Consistency. Change a phone number once; every screen that uses it shows the new number. Security. Only authorised users see sensitive fields (an admin sees marks; office staff see names). Integrity. Rules stop duplicate roll numbers and empty primary keys.

topics.title: 4.2 Database Components (Tables, Records, Fields)
topics.learn: The basic structure is a table (also called a relation): rows and columns, like a spreadsheet, holding facts about one kind of thing (Students, Teachers, Books). A record (row, tuple) is one complete instance — everything about Ali. A field (column, attribute) is one kind of fact — the whole Name column, or the whole Grade column.

topics.title: 4.3.1 Keys and Integrity Constraints
topics.learn: A key is a field (or a set of fields) that uniquely identifies records and links tables. Integrity constraints are the rules that keep those keys honest. Candidate key. Any field (or combination) that could uniquely identify a row. A table may have several. In an Employee table: EmpID, EmpLicense# and EmpPassport are all candidate keys. Primary key (PK). The one candidate you actually choose. Rules: unique, never NULL, only one PK per table (it may be a composite of two columns). Example: EmpID. Alternate key. The leftover candidate keys. After EmpID is chosen, EmpLicense# and EmpPassport become alternate keys — still unique, just not “the” identifier. Foreign key (FK). A field in this table that refers to the PK of another table. It may contain duplicates (many employees in one department) and, in some designs, NULL.

topics.title: 4.3 Relational Database Management System (RDBMS)
topics.learn: An RDBMS stores data in several tables and uses primary and foreign keys to keep relationships. Banks, universities and NADRA use RDBMS software. Extra strengths on top of a plain DBMS: Reduces redundancy by splitting data into related tables. Supports many users at once, with permissions. Is queried with SQL (Structured Query Language) — a standard language of SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.

topics.title: 4.5 Referential Integrity
topics.learn: Referential integrity means every foreign-key value in a child table must match an existing primary-key value in the parent — or be NULL if the design allows it. It stops orphan records. If Result.StudentID is a FK to Student.StudentID, you cannot type Result for student 999 if 999 is not in Student. You also cannot delete student 101 while results for 101 still exist — unless you first handle those child rows.

topics.title: 4.6 Relational Schema Development
topics.learn: A relational schema is the formal written design of the database: table names, fields, primary keys, foreign keys and how tables relate. You write it before clicking around in Access. It defines (1) how data is split into tables, (2) which columns each table has, (3) which fields are PK/FK, (4) the relationships. Benefits: less redundancy, integrity planned in advance, easier to grow later.

topics.title: 4.7 Case Study — Library Management System
topics.learn: A college library needs a database. Walk the seven steps examiners expect. Step 1 — Requirements. A book has ID, title, author, publisher. A member (student/teacher) has ID, name, contact. A member can borrow many books; a book can be borrowed by different members over time. Record Issue Date and Return Date. Step 2 — Entities. Book, Member. (Borrowing will need a third entity in step 6.) Step 3 — Attributes. Book: BookID (PK), Title, Author, Publisher. Member: MemberID (PK), Name, ContactInfo. Step 4 — Relationship. Member borrows Book. Step 5 — Cardinality. One member borrows many books over time; one book is borrowed by many members over time → M:N. Step 6 — Resolve M:N. Add junction entity BorrowRecord: BorrowID (PK), MemberID (FK), BookID (FK), IssueDate, ReturnDate. Now Member 1—M BorrowRecord M—1 Book (two 1:M links). Step 7 — Final schema.

topics.learn: Plan first (4.9.1): purpose, field list, data type of each field, which field is the PK. Datasheet View (4.9.2) — fast, spreadsheet-like, good for beginners, weak on rules. Limitation: you cannot easily say “Marks cannot exceed 100”. Professionals use Design View. Design View (4.9.3) — full control before any data is typed. Create tab → Table. A blank grid appears. Double-click Field1, Field2, … to rename. Type data; Access guesses the data type. Create tab → Table Design. Type each Field Name (StudentID, Name, …). Pick the Data Type from the dropdown. Right-click the unique field → Primary Key (key icon). Save the table.

topics.title: 4.10 Designing Forms for Data Manipulation
topics.learn: A form is the screen people actually type into. It cuts errors and can show validation messages. Every form must have a data source — a table or a query. A form with no source has nowhere to save. Form Wizard (the exam method): Create tab → Form Wizard. Select the table (e.g. Student). Move fields with > (one) or >> (all). Choose layout. Columnar = one record at a time, best for data entry. Name it (“Student Registration”) → Finish.

Sketchnote کھولو اور Grouping والا حصہ انگلی سے دباؤ۔ میں یہ line پڑھ کر نہیں گزر رہی۔ Line یہ کہتی ہے: گروپ بائی ایک جیسے ریکارڈ جوڑتا ہے، پھر COUNT، SUM، AVG، MAX، MIN سے خلاصہ نکلتا ہے۔۔ Intermediate student کے لیے مطلب یہ ہے کہ نام لکھ دینا کافی نہیں۔ تمہیں بتانا ہے کہ یہ rule کب کام کرتا ہے اور کب نہیں کرتا۔ Grouping English میں رہے گا۔ اس کا جوڑ aggregate سے ہے۔ اگر examiner پوچھے کہ فرق کیا ہے، تو یوں جواب دو: ایکسیس میں Σ بٹن Total قطار کھولتا ہے۔۔ اب دس سیکنڈ رکو۔ اپنی کاپی بند کرو اور Grouping کی ایک example بولو۔ پھر sketchnote کھول کر دیکھو کہ تمہاری example اسی rule پر کھڑی ہے یا نہیں۔ Minute 2. اب aggregate کو غلط تعریف سے الگ کرو۔ لوگ اکثر aggregate اور Grouping کو ایک ہی چیز سمجھ لیتے ہیں۔ Sketchnote کہتی ہے: ایکسیس میں Σ بٹن Total قطار کھولتا ہے۔۔ اس کا مطلب یہ نہیں کہ Check: CS marks 80, 85 → average (80+85)/2 = 82.5.۔ ایک mark تب ملتا ہے جب تم aggregate کا نام اور ایک سچی بات لکھو۔ تین marks تب ملتے ہیں جب نام کے بعد reason ہو، اور reason ایکسیس میں Σ بٹن Total قطار کھولتا ہے۔ سے آئے۔ پانچ marks کے لیے وہی reason، پھر ایک local example، پھر diagram یا table کا اشارہ۔ Local example school، phone، JazzCash، یا load-shedding سے دو، مگر term English میں لکھو۔ اگر example Grouping کے rule پر چلی جائے تو جواب غلط ہے۔ دوبارہ چیک کرو۔ Minute 3. Diagram اور table کی طرف آؤ، paragraph دوبارہ نہ پڑھو۔ Picture یا row یہ بتا رہی ہے: Check: CS marks 80, 85 → average (80+85)/2 = 82.5.۔ Intermediate paper میں figure تب نمبر دیتی ہے جب labels English میں ہوں اور تم بتاؤ کہ arrow یا column کیا فرق دکھا رہا ہے۔ Grouping والی طرف ایک حقیقت رکھو، aggregate والی طرف دوسری۔ دوسری حقیقت یہ ہے: IT 70, 82 → 76.0.۔ اب ایک row زور سے بول دو، پھر آنکھ بند کرکے وہی row دوبارہ بول دو۔ جو لفظ بھولے، وہی exam میں کٹتا ہے۔ اسے ابھی sketchnote پر نشان لگاو۔ Minute 4. topics.title: 5.1 Introduction to Computing Impacts
topics.learn: Computing means using computers and computer-based devices to store, process and share information. Today computing is an important part of your daily life. You use computers, mobile phones, the internet and smart devices almost everywhere — at home, in college and on the road. In Pakistan, computing is becoming vital (very necessary) in: An impact is the effect something has on people and society. Computing has positive impacts (speed, convenience, new jobs) and negative impacts (privacy risks, addiction, job loss). In this chapter you will study three key technologies first — AI, IoT and Data Analytics — and then their uses and impacts. Schools and colleges — online admissions, e-books, online results of the Sindh boards. Hospitals — computerised patient records, digital X-rays, online appointment systems. Banks — ATMs, mobile banking apps, Raast instant payments, JazzCash and Easypaisa wallets. Farms — weather forecasts on mobile phones, soil sensors, tube-well control. Industries — automatic machines in textile mills in Karachi, Hyderabad and Faisalabad.

topics.title: 5.1.1 Artificial Intelligence (AI)
topics.learn: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the ability of a computer system to perform tasks that normally need human thinking, such as recognising faces, understanding language and making decisions. Understand the name in two parts: AI systems use data to make decisions. The more good data an AI system sees, the better it becomes at recognising patterns (repeating features) and predicting what to do. Examples from the source: More Pakistani examples: Google Maps predicting traffic on Shahrah-e-Faisal, Urdu voice typing on your phone, banks flagging a suspicious card transaction, and AI tools that translate English into Urdu. Artificial — it is created by humans; it is not natural. Intelligence — it can perform tasks that require thinking. Face recognition on a mobile phone to unlock the screen. YouTube suggesting videos based on your interests. Chatbots answering questions on a website (for example, a bank's help chat).

topics.title: 5.1.2 Internet of Things (IoT) & Components
topics.learn: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a system in which physical devices are connected to the Internet and can collect and share data to perform tasks automatically. The "things" are ordinary objects — watches, cameras, cars, fans, water pumps — that have been given sensors and an internet connection so they can "talk" to each other and to us. Source example: A smartwatch collects your heart-rate data and sends it to your mobile phone, where it is displayed.

topics.title: 5.1.3 Data Analytics & Components
topics.learn: Data Analytics is the process of collecting, organising, cleaning, studying and presenting data to find useful information. It helps people make better decisions. Data means raw facts and figures (for example, "72, 45, 88"). Information is data that has been processed so it has meaning ("Ali scored 72%; he passed"). Data Analytics is the bridge from data to information. Source example: A college collects exam marks, calculates percentages, and identifies which students need extra help. This entire process is Data Analytics.

topics.title: 5.2 Uses of IoT in Different Areas
topics.learn: IoT improves efficiency (doing more with less effort), saves time, and enhances the overall quality of life. It plays a significant role in developing modern infrastructure (the basic systems of a country — roads, power, water, hospitals). The source lists six areas.
topics.urdu: IoT کارکردگی بہتر بناتا ہے، وقت بچاتا ہے اور زندگی کا معیار بلند کرتا ہے۔ اسمارٹ شہروں میں ٹریفک سگنل اور اسٹریٹ لائٹس خود کار ہوتی ہیں، اسپتالوں میں مریضوں کا ڈیٹا براہِ راست ڈاکٹر تک پہنچتا ہے، اور کھیتوں میں مٹی کی نمی کے سینسر بتاتے ہیں کہ فصل کو پانی چاہیے یا نہیں، جس سے سندھ اور پنجاب میں پانی کی بچت ہوتی ہے۔

topics.title: 5.2.1 Scope of AI in Education in Pakistan
topics.learn: Artificial Intelligence is gradually becoming an important part of Pakistan's education system, improving teaching, learning and administration (managing the school: admissions, records, timetables). Practical uses: Benefits: Major challenges in Pakistan: Learning Management Systems (LMS) — online platforms (e.g. Google Classroom, Moodle) where teachers post lessons and assignments; AI features can recommend lessons to each student. Automated grading and digital testing — MCQ tests marked instantly by computer. AI-based career counselling — software that studies a student's marks and interests and suggests suitable fields. Helps students learn at their own speed. Identifies students who need extra help. Supports students with disabilities (Assistive AI), e.g. text-to-speech for a visually impaired student. Limited internet access in rural areas. Lack of computers and digital devices for all students. Need for proper teacher training to use AI tools. Data privacy and security issues — students' personal data must be protected.

topics.title: 5.2.2 Career Connection in IoT and AI
topics.learn: Learning computing skills opens doors to many employers in Pakistan: software houses (e.g. in Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad technology parks), telecom companies (Jazz, Telenor), banks, and government IT departments (e.g. NADRA, provincial IT boards). Key skills needed: IoT Engineer: designs smart systems and connected devices (e.g. a smart irrigation kit). Data Analyst: analyses the data generated by IoT systems and produces reports. Programming — Python, C++. Networking — Wi-Fi, protocols (rules for how devices communicate). Electronics — sensors and circuits. Problem-solving.

topics.title: 5.3 Information Sources (Primary, Secondary, Tertiary)
topics.learn: Information sources are ways to find knowledge and data. The internet has vast information, but not all of it is accurate. Sources are divided into three main categories. 1. Primary sources give original, firsthand information straight from people, events or official records. They are highly authentic (genuine).Examples: interviews, photographs, diaries, NADRA official records. 2. Secondary sources contain information that has already been collected and explained by someone else. They summarise or analyse primary data.Examples: textbooks, news reports, research papers, Pakistan Bureau of Statistics reports. 3. Tertiary sources provide highly summarised and organised information derived from both primary and secondary sources. They are used for quick reference.Examples: encyclopedias, Wikipedia, dictionaries, handbooks.

topics.title: 5.4 Impacts of Computing in Various Fields
topics.learn: Computing has drastically changed society. It makes life faster and more connected, but it also brings challenges like privacy risks and technology addiction. For every field, think of both sides.

topics.title: 5.5 Assistive Technologies
topics.learn: Assistive technologies are devices, software and systems that help people with disabilities or functional limitations (difficulty in seeing, hearing, moving, speaking, remembering, etc.). They allow more people to participate equally in school, work and society. There are four categories:

topics.title: 5.5.1 Importance of Assistive Technologies
topics.learn: Assistive technologies are important for three main reasons: Equal access to education: Screen readers allow blind students to read digital textbooks equally with their peers (classmates). Independence in daily life: Mobility aids reduce the need for constant human assistance — a person in a smart wheelchair can go to the market without someone pushing. Social inclusion: They break down barriers, allowing individuals to work, study and socialise confidently.

topics.title: 5.5.2 Career Connection in Assistive Tech
topics.learn: Designing assistive technology is a highly rewarding career path — you earn a living while improving people's lives. UX means user experience (how easy and pleasant a product is to use); UI means user interface (the screens and buttons you interact with). Accessibility means designing so that everyone, including people with disabilities, can use it.

topics.title: 6.1 Introduction to Digital Literacy
topics.learn: Digital literacy is the ability to understand and use digital devices, the internet, and online tools in a safe, effective, and responsible manner. Look at the three key words: In our increasingly digital world, digital literacy is essential for everyone, not only for computer experts. It enables you to: Safe – you protect yourself and others online (for example, you do not share passwords or private details). Effective – you get the job done well (for example, you find the right information quickly). Responsible – you use information honestly and fairly (for example, you do not copy someone else's work or spread false news). find information, communicate with others, produce digital content, and solve problems through technology.

topics.title: 6.2 Digital Literacy in the Information Age
topics.learn: The Information Age is the period we live in now, where vast amounts of data are produced, shared and accessed instantly through the internet, mobile devices and digital platforms (websites, apps, social media). Simply having access to technology is not enough. Owning a smartphone does not make you good at using information. You must develop the skills to understand, manage and use information wisely. Digital literacy goes beyond basic computer skills. It involves three kinds of ability: Together these abilities help you function successfully in a digital society.

topics.title: 6.3 Types of Data
topics.learn: Data means facts, numbers, words or observations that we collect. The data gathered through a survey, an investigation or a classroom project can be described in two ways: qualitatively or quantitatively. Knowing the difference is critical, because each type is analysed in a different way. Going a little further (background). Quantitative data is sometimes split into two kinds: Also note: a question with fixed categories (e.g. "Which activity do you use your phone for most? Lectures / Notes / Social media / Games") gives categories that you can count. In this chapter's case study such answers are treated as quantitative (categories), because you count how many students chose each option. Discrete data can only take separate, countable values, e.g. number of students in a class (35, 36 – never 35.5). Continuous data can take any value in a range and is measured, e.g. height (162.4 cm) or time online (2.75 hours).

topics.title: 6.4.1 – 6.4.2 Interviews and Surveys
topics.learn: An interview is a planned conversation used to gather information directly from a person. Strength: you get deep, detailed answers and can ask follow-up questions ("Why do you say that?"). Weakness: it takes a lot of time, so you can only interview a few people. It may be one-to-one (you and one person) or in a small group. Questions are planned in advance, so you do not forget anything important. Answers are usually qualitative (opinions, reasons, experiences). A survey (or questionnaire) is useful when the same set of questions needs to be asked to many people. It may be on paper or created with digital tools such as Google Forms or Microsoft Forms. Note: online survey tools automatically collect responses and display basic charts, which makes data analysis much easier.

Sketchnote کھولو اور interview والا حصہ انگلی سے دباؤ۔ میں یہ line پڑھ کر نہیں گزر رہی۔ Line یہ کہتی ہے: انٹرویو ایک منصوبہ بند گفتگو ہے جس میں کسی ایک فرد یا چھوٹے گروہ سے براہِ راست معلومات حاصل کی جاتی ہیں؛ اس کے جوابات عموماً کیفیتی ہوتے ہیں۔۔ Intermediate student کے لیے مطلب یہ ہے کہ نام لکھ دینا کافی نہیں۔ تمہیں بتانا ہے کہ یہ rule کب کام کرتا ہے اور کب نہیں کرتا۔ interview English میں رہے گا۔ اس کا جوڑ planned conversation سے ہے۔ اگر examiner پوچھے کہ فرق کیا ہے، تو یوں جواب دو: سروے میں ایک ہی سوالات بہت سے لوگوں سے پوچھے جاتے ہیں، کاغذ پر یا Google Forms جیسے ڈیجیٹل ٹولز کے ذریعے، جو جوابات خودکار طور پر جمع کر کے چارٹ بھی دکھاتے ہیں۔۔ اب دس سیکنڈ رکو۔ اپنی کاپی بند کرو اور interview کی ایک example بولو۔ پھر sketchnote کھول کر دیکھو کہ تمہاری example اسی rule پر کھڑی ہے یا نہیں۔ Minute 2. اب planned conversation کو غلط تعریف سے الگ کرو۔ لوگ اکثر planned conversation اور directly from a person کو ایک ہی چیز سمجھ لیتے ہیں۔ Sketchnote کہتی ہے: سروے میں ایک ہی سوالات بہت سے لوگوں سے پوچھے جاتے ہیں، کاغذ پر یا Google Forms جیسے ڈیجیٹل ٹولز کے ذریعے، جو جوابات خودکار طور پر جمع کر کے چارٹ بھی دکھاتے ہیں۔۔ اس کا مطلب یہ نہیں کہ اچھا سوال واضح، مختصر، غیر جانبدار اور ایک وقت میں ایک ہی بات کے بارے میں ہوتا ہے۔۔ ایک mark تب ملتا ہے جب تم planned conversation کا نام اور ایک سچی بات لکھو۔ تین marks تب ملتے ہیں جب نام کے بعد reason ہو، اور reason سروے میں ایک ہی سوالات بہت سے لوگوں سے پوچھے جاتے ہیں، کاغذ پر یا Google Forms جیسے ڈیجیٹل ٹولز کے ذریعے، جو جوابات خودکار طور پر جمع کر کے چارٹ بھی دکھاتے ہیں۔ سے آئے۔ پانچ marks کے لیے وہی reason، پھر ایک local example، پھر diagram یا table کا اشارہ۔ Local example school، phone، JazzCash، یا load-shedding سے دو، مگر term English میں لکھو۔ اگر example directly from a person کے rule پر چلی جائے تو جواب غلط ہے۔ دوبارہ چیک کرو۔ Minute 3. Diagram اور table کی طرف آؤ، paragraph دوبارہ نہ پڑھو۔ Picture یا row یہ بتا رہی ہے: اچھا سوال واضح، مختصر، غیر جانبدار اور ایک وقت میں ایک ہی بات کے بارے میں ہوتا ہے۔۔ Intermediate paper میں figure تب نمبر دیتی ہے جب labels English میں ہوں اور تم بتاؤ کہ arrow یا column کیا فرق دکھا رہا ہے۔ directly from a person والی طرف ایک حقیقت رکھو، one-to-one والی طرف دوسری۔ دوسری حقیقت یہ ہے: An interview is a planned conversation used to gather information directly from a person.۔ اب ایک row زور سے بول دو، پھر آنکھ بند کرکے وہی row دوبارہ بول دو۔ جو لفظ بھولے، وہی exam میں کٹتا ہے۔ اسے ابھی sketchnote پر نشان لگاو۔ Minute 4. Example کو آہستہ چلاؤ، جیسے تم کسی دوست کو سمجھا رہے ہو۔ شروع کی بات یہ ہے: An interview is a planned conversation used to gather information directly from a person.۔ اگلا قدم خود نکالو، میں answer ابھی نہیں دے رہی۔ سوچنے کے لیے رک جاؤ۔ اب جواب ملا کر دیکھو: Strength: you get deep, detailed answers and can ask follow-up questions ("Why do you say that?").۔ اگر تمہارا قدم اس سے مختلف ہے تو پوچھو کہ input وہی ہے یا تم نے one-to-one کا rule بدل دیا۔ Code ہو تو syntax مت رٹو۔ ہر line کا مقصد بولو: data اندر کیا آیا، decision کہاں ہوا، result کیا بدلا۔ one-to-one اور small group دونوں English میں رہیں، وضاحت Urdu میں دو۔ Minute 5. غلطی کا کلینک۔ Intermediate student small group کی definition لکھ کر رک جاتا ہے۔ Paper یہ نہیں پوچھتا کہ تمہیں sentence یاد ہے۔ Paper پوچھتا ہے کہ sentence اس case پر لگتا ہے یا نہیں۔ غلط اطلاق تب ہوتا ہے جب تم Strength: you get deep, detailed answers and can ask follow-up questions ("Why do you say that?"). کو Weakness: it takes a lot of time, so you can only interview a few people. پر چسپاں کر دو۔ صحیح چیک یہ ہے: پہلے بتائو کہ case count ہے یا measure، name ہے یا process، input ہے یا output۔ پھر small group رکھو۔ اگر case planned in advance کا ہے تو پہلا نام کاٹ دو۔ جواب کے آخر میں ایک لائن لکھو: اس لیے یہ small group ہے، کیونکہ Strength: you get deep, detailed answers and can ask follow-up questions ("Why do you say that?").۔ Minute 6. تین marks کا جواب ابھی بناؤ، کتاب بند رکھ کر۔ پہلی لائن: planned in advance وہ ہے جس کے بارے میں sketchnote کہتی ہے، Weakness: it takes a lot of time, so you can only interview a few people.۔ دوسری لائن: یہ interview نہیں، کیونکہ It may be one-to-one (you and one person) or in a small group.۔ تیسری لائن: میری example۔ example میں نام English، صورتحال اپنی۔ اب کتاب کھولو اور تینوں لائنیں sketchnote سے ملاؤ۔ جو لائن board پر نہیں بنتی، اسے کاٹ دو۔ جو لائن بنتی ہے، اسے دوبارہ آہستہ بولو تاکہ زبان پر بیٹھ جائے۔ یہ reading نہیں۔ یہ وہ جواب ہے جو تم ہال میں لکھو گے۔ Minute 7. Digital Literacy کے اندر 6.4.1 – 6.4.2 Interviews and Surveys کہاں کھڑا ہے۔ Golden topic ہے، اس پر paper میں comparison مانگا جاتا ہے۔ پچھلا idea بغیر اس کے ادھورا رہتا ہے، اور اگلا idea اس کے بغیر شروع نہیں ہوتا۔ جوڑ یہ ہے: It may be one-to-one (you and one person) or in a small group.۔ اسی جوڑ کو planned conversation تک لے جاؤ: Questions are planned in advance, so you do not forget anything important.۔ جب تم chapter revise کرو تو ہر topic کا ایک جملہ اور ایک term کافی نہیں۔ تمہارے پاس interview کا جملہ، اس کا الٹ، اور ایک example ہونا چاہیے۔ اب sketchnote کے عنوان کو چھپاؤ اور صرف diagram یا پہلی line دیکھ کر عنوان خود بولو۔ Minute 8. آخری پکڑ، پھر اگلے حصے سے پہلے۔ اگر تم سے ابھی پوچھیں کہ planned conversation ایک لائن میں کیا ہے، تو یہ مت بولو کہ مجھے پورا پیرا یاد ہے۔ یہ بولو: Questions are planned in advance, so you do not forget anything important.۔ اگر پوچھیں کہ مثال دو، تو Answers are usually qualitative (opinions, reasons, experiences). کو اپنی مثال بناؤ، بشرطیکہ وہ planned conversation کا rule توڑے نہیں۔ اگر پوچھیں کہ غلطی کیا ہوتی ہے، تو بولو کہ student planned conversation اور directly from a person کو ملا دیتا ہے۔ دس سیکنڈ خاموشی۔ پھر تین لفظ English میں اور ایک جملہ Urdu میں۔ بس۔ اگلی minute اسی topic کی اگلی تہہ ہے۔ Minute 9. topics.learn: A prototype is a simple early version of a product, model or solution. It allows an idea to be tested before time and effort are spent on the final version. Users try the prototype and give feedback, and this feedback becomes useful data for improvement. Example: Before building a full school app, you draw the screens on paper (or make a few clickable screens in a design tool) and ask five classmates to try "finding the timetable". You note where they get confused. In observation, the researcher watches what people do or what happens in a situation and records the results carefully. No direct questions are asked. The data may be qualitative (written notes, e.g. "students push in the queue") or quantitative (counts, e.g. "42 students bought samosas in 10 minutes"). Why use it? People sometimes say one thing and do another. Observation shows what really happens. A simulation is a computer-based model of a real situation. Variables (the things that can change, like speed, temperature or number of people) can be changed to see what happens. Simulations are highly useful when real experiments are costly, risky or difficult to perform. Examples: a flight simulator for training pilots (real crashes are dangerous); a traffic simulation to test what happens if a new signal is added (changing real roads is costly); a weather model to predict a cyclone (you cannot experiment with real weather).

topics.title: 6.5 Primary and Secondary Data
topics.learn: Whenever you use data, it is important to know where it came from. The source affects how much control the researcher had over collecting it, and how confidently the results can be used.
topics.urdu: بنیادی ڈیٹا (Primary Data) محقق خود کسی خاص مقصد کے لیے براہِ راست جمع کرتا ہے، مثلاً سروے، انٹرویو یا مشاہدہ۔ ثانوی ڈیٹا (Secondary Data) پہلے ہی کسی اور نے جمع کیا ہوتا ہے اور اسے نئے مقصد کے لیے دوبارہ استعمال کیا جاتا ہے، جیسے کتابیں، رپورٹس اور آن لائن ڈیٹا بیس۔ بنیادی ڈیٹا پر محقق کا کنٹرول زیادہ اور ثانوی ڈیٹا پر کم ہوتا ہے۔

topics.title: 6.6 Designing a Data-Collection Approach
topics.learn: Before collecting data, a researcher must have a plan. A plan makes sure that the information gathered is accurate, relevant (related to the question) and useful. Follow these eight steps in order: Define the research question clearly. What exactly do you want to find out? Decide the type of data needed: quantitative, qualitative, or both. Select suitable methods (survey, interview, observation). Choose the sample or target group – the people who will give you data. Prepare the tools such as forms, questions and observation sheets. Collect the data carefully and accurately. Store the data digitally in a spreadsheet and keep a backup. Follow ethical practice and respect privacy. Consent is mandatory (you must get permission).

topics.title: 6.7 Presenting Data Using Digital Tools: 6.7.1 Spreadsheets and 6.7.2 Presentations
topics.learn: Collecting data is only one part of the work. You must also present your findings so that others can understand them quickly and easily. Digital tools make this much easier. The four main tools are spreadsheets, presentations, infographics and reports. Spreadsheets such as MS Excel, Google Sheets and Apple Numbers arrange information in rows (horizontal, numbered 1, 2, 3…) and columns (vertical, lettered A, B, C…). The box where a row and column meet is a cell, named by its column and row, e.g. B2. With a spreadsheet you can: A formula always starts with =. A range such as B2:B4 means "cells B2 to B4". Enter data systematically (one record per row). Calculate totals, averages and percentages. Sort (arrange in order) and filter (show only some rows) records. Create charts and graphs automatically. Presentation software such as PowerPoint, Google Slides and Canva helps you explain findings to an audience in an organised way. Good practice: Spreadsheets and presentations work together: you make a chart from the spreadsheet data and insert it into the slides. Begin with a clear title and the research question. Use short bullet points instead of long paragraphs. Include tables, charts and key findings. Keep the design simple and readable (large font, few colours).

topics.title: 6.7.3 – 6.7.4 Infographics and Reports
topics.learn: An infographic (information + graphic) is a visual way of presenting information, facts or data so that people can understand the main idea quickly and easily. Tools such as Canva, Power BI or Tableau can be used. A good infographic should: Simplify complex concepts. Highlight the most important findings and results. Use clear visuals, limited text and accurate information. Reports are structured documents used to present collected data, findings, analysis and conclusions. Tools like MS Word or Google Docs are standard. A good report should: Optional: you may use AI tools carefully to improve wording, but always review for accuracy. AI can make mistakes or invent facts, and you are responsible for what you submit. Start with a clear title, introduction and purpose. Present the collected data using tables or charts. Explain findings in simple language. Include conclusions and recommendations based on the data. Visual rule of thumb: a good chart or infographic can explain complex data faster than a long paragraph. However, visuals must always be accurate and based strictly on the real data collected – never exaggerated.

topics.title: 6.8 Case Study: Digital Inquiry Project
topics.learn: This case study shows how to apply all the ideas of this chapter to solve a real-world problem from start to finish. An inquiry is an investigation to find the answer to a question. Research question: "How does daily mobile phone use affect the study habits of students?" Scenario: Students notice classmates using phones during free periods and while studying. Some say phones help them learn; others say phones waste time. The class must investigate whether phone use helps or harms study habits.

topics.title: 6.8 Steps 1 – 3: Advanced Search and Methodology
topics.learn: Students first search for background information using search engines (such as Google or Bing). They use advanced search operators – special symbols or words typed into the search box – to narrow down results and find reliable secondary data. Other useful operators (background): - (minus) excludes a word, e.g. phone addiction -game; OR finds either word, e.g. smartphone OR mobile; site:.gov.pk searches only Pakistani government websites. Source evaluation checklist. Before trusting a source, ask: Is the author/organisation clearly mentioned? Is the information recent? Is the website reliable (.edu, .gov, research-based)? Does the source provide facts/references, or is it biased (one-sided, trying to sell something)? Students decide what kind of primary data they will collect: Quantitative: number of hours used daily; percentage who feel distracted. topics.title: 6.8 Steps 4 – 6: Survey Preparation and Primary Data Collection
topics.learn: Design clear, unbiased questions. Each question is linked to the type of data it produces: The sample is the group of people who provide the data. It is usually impossible to ask everyone (the whole population), so a smaller group is chosen. The students decide to survey 40 Class XI students from different sections to get a representative mix of habits. topics.title: 6.8 Steps 7 – 9: Secondary Data and Spreadsheet Organisation
topics.learn: Students include a reliable online article stating that "excessive screen time lowers concentration." They will compare this secondary data with their own primary survey results. If both agree, the conclusion is stronger. If they disagree, the students must think about why (for example, a different age group or country). topics.learn: To analyse means to study the data carefully to find patterns and trends. By looking at the spreadsheet and charts, the group identifies: Most students (the majority) use phones for 3–5 hours daily. Half use it for educational purposes (lectures/notes). A clear trend: students who use phones mostly for entertainment report much higher distraction levels than those who use them for study. A conclusion answers the research question using the evidence: "The research shows mobile phones have both positive and negative effects. They provide access to learning materials. However, excessive use of social media and gaming reduces concentration. Therefore, phones should not be banned, but managed wisely." Recommendations are practical suggestions based on the data. The students recommend: Turn off social media notifications while studying. Set daily screen-time limits. Take physical breaks from screens to protect health.

topics.learn: A digital artefact is a final product created using digital technologies. Students must create one final artefact that answers the original research question. It is not just a decorated file; it must present evidence and conclusions. A dashboard is an interactive screen of charts; the viewer can click filters (e.g. "show only Commerce students") and the charts update.

topics.title: 1.1 Fundamentals of Human-Computer Interaction
topics.learn: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) is the study and design of technology so that it serves people. An HCI system is easy to use, efficient, and responsive to human needs. HCI is also known as CHI (Computer-Human Interface) or MMI (Man-Machine Interaction). The three names mean the same idea: the meeting point of a person and a machine. HCI is not only "making a pretty screen". It asks: Can a student in Hyderabad find results on the school portal in 30 seconds? Can a grandmother send JazzCash without help? Can a person standing at an outdoor ATM in bright sunlight read the buttons?

Sketchnote کھولو اور Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) والا حصہ انگلی سے دباؤ۔ میں یہ line پڑھ کر نہیں گزر رہی۔ Line یہ کہتی ہے: HCI کا مطلب ہے ٹیکنالوجی کو اس طرح ڈیزائن کرنا کہ وہ انسانوں کے لیے فائدہ مند، آسان اور مؤثر ہو۔۔ Intermediate student کے لیے مطلب یہ ہے کہ نام لکھ دینا کافی نہیں۔ تمہیں بتانا ہے کہ یہ rule کب کام کرتا ہے اور کب نہیں کرتا۔ Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) English میں رہے گا۔ اس کا جوڑ serves people سے ہے۔ اگر examiner پوچھے کہ فرق کیا ہے، تو یوں جواب دو: اسے CHI یا MMI بھی کہتے ہیں۔۔ اب دس سیکنڈ رکو۔ اپنی کاپی بند کرو اور Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) کی ایک example بولو۔ پھر sketchnote کھول کر دیکھو کہ تمہاری example اسی rule پر کھڑی ہے یا نہیں۔ Minute 2. اب serves people کو غلط تعریف سے الگ کرو۔ لوگ اکثر serves people اور CHI کو ایک ہی چیز سمجھ لیتے ہیں۔ Sketchnote کہتی ہے: اسے CHI یا MMI بھی کہتے ہیں۔۔ اس کا مطلب یہ نہیں کہ انسان اور کمپیوٹر پانچ حسّی راستوں سے بات کرتے ہیں: بصارت، چھونا، سننا، آواز اور مکانی حرکت۔۔ ایک mark تب ملتا ہے جب تم serves people کا نام اور ایک سچی بات لکھو۔ تین marks تب ملتے ہیں جب نام کے بعد reason ہو، اور reason اسے CHI یا MMI بھی کہتے ہیں۔ سے آئے۔ پانچ marks کے لیے وہی reason، پھر ایک local example، پھر diagram یا table کا اشارہ۔ Local example school، phone، JazzCash، یا load-shedding سے دو، مگر term English میں لکھو۔ اگر example CHI کے rule پر چلی جائے تو جواب غلط ہے۔ دوبارہ چیک کرو۔ Minute 3. topics.title: 1.1.1 Traditional Interaction and 1.1.2 Natural Interaction
topics.learn: 1.1.1 Traditional interaction is the basic way people use everyday devices. It relies on standard input and output: a mouse, a keyboard, a keypad, a monitor, speakers, or a simple touchscreen tap and swipe. 1.1.2 Natural interaction is advanced, smart technology that lets people interact without a mouse or keyboard. It feels more human — you speak, move, or show your face, and the system understands. Computer: moving a mouse and typing on a keyboard; output via monitor and speakers. Smartphone (traditional use): tapping and swiping on a touchscreen; output via screen lighting and vibrations. Voice: speaking commands into a device (for example, "Alexa, play a song"). Body and gesture: facial recognition to unlock a phone, or playing VR games by waving hands.

topics.learn: HCI is used to design and develop interactive systems such as desktop applications, websites and mobile apps. These are human-centred solutions built to meet user needs across many domains of life. A domain is an area of daily activity — health, money, school, talking to people. When you design for a domain, you design for that domain's users, tasks and risks. A mistake on a games app is annoying. A mistake on a medical or banking screen can harm a person or lose money. That is why examiners treat this topic as golden.

topics.title: 1.3 Components of HCI
topics.learn: HCI relies on several primary components that work together. If one component is weak, the whole interaction feels broken. The first four are the people, the machine, the conversation, and the job to be done.

topics.title: Interface Types, Environment and Feedback
topics.learn: Components v–vii complete the HCI picture: the look of the controls, the place where you use them, and the signals that tell you "it worked" or "try again". The user interface is the medium through which humans interact with computer systems. The environment is the real-world setting where a person uses a computer system. It is shaped by: Feedback is the signal or response given to confirm or guide actions. Graphical User Interface (GUI): visual elements such as windows, icons and menus (Windows OS, Android). Command-Line Interface (CLI): text-based typing (MS-DOS, Linux terminal). Touch interface: tapping, swiping, pinching (smartphones, tablets). Voice User Interface (VUI): spoken commands (smart speakers). Natural User Interface (NUI): gestures, body movements or immersive environments (VR headsets, Microsoft Kinect). Physical conditions — an ATM outdoors in sunlight, heat, noise, rain. Social conditions — a quiet classroom, a crowded bazaar, privacy at a PIN pad. Technical hardware — slow college Wi-Fi, a cracked phone screen, an old browser.

topics.title: 1.4 Importance of HCI
topics.learn: HCI ensures that machines are approachable and usable, turning complex technology into everyday tools. Good design makes technology simple and enjoyable (touchscreens). Poor design causes confusion and risks (unclear buttons on medical devices). This is why HCI is not optional decoration. A confusing JazzCash confirm button can send money to the wrong number. A confusing school-portal "Submit" can lock a student out of an online exam. Importance questions in the board exam expect the five implications below, each with a sentence of explanation.

topics.title: 1.5 Accessibility Principles
topics.learn: Accessibility principles are HCI guidelines that ensure digital systems are usable by all individuals, including people with diverse physical, sensory and cognitive abilities. They remove barriers to create equal access. Accessibility is not a "special extra". It is how you make sure a student with low vision, a shopkeeper who cannot use a mouse, or a colour-blind driver can still complete the task.
topics.urdu: رسائی پذیری (Accessibility) کے اصول یقینی بناتے ہیں کہ ہر انسان سسٹم استعمال کر سکے، بشمول مختلف جسمانی، حسّی اور ذہنی صلاحیتوں والے افراد۔ پانچ اصول: اونچا تضاد (کنٹراسٹ)، پڑھنے میں آسان فونٹ، صرف رنگ پر انحصار نہ کرنا، کی بورڈ سمیت متبادل نیویگیشن، اور معلومات کو نظر، آواز اور لمس کئی شکلوں میں دینا۔

topics.title: 1.6 Need Analysis for Interface Design
topics.learn: Need analysis is the process of identifying the gap between the existing situation and the desired outcome. In HCI it is done before designing a UI, so that you understand users' goals, tasks, abilities and expectations. If you skip need analysis, you guess. Guessing is how a school portal ends up with 40 menus and no "Download date sheet" button on the home screen.

topics.title: 1.7 Human-Computer Interaction Problems
topics.learn: HCI problems are common difficulties that stop users from using technology smoothly. They happen when systems fail to meet human needs or cognitive limits. Cognitive limits means the mind can only hold and process so much at once — if an app asks you to remember three SMS codes at the same time, it has gone past that limit. Board answers score well when you name the problem, explain it in one line, and give a concrete example (the source examples are safe; a matching local example is even better).

topics.title: 1.8 Methods for Improving HCI
topics.learn: Once you can name an HCI problem, you fix it with a matching method. The source lists eight methods. Learn each with its tiny example — they pair almost one-to-one with Section 1.7. User-centred design (UCD) means the real user's goals drive every decision, and you trial (pilot-test) the design with those users instead of guessing in an office. Responsive design means the layout rearranges itself for phone, tablet and PC, instead of staying a laptop-only page. Enhance usability: simplify navigation (a clear "Buy Now" button). Strengthen accessibility: support disabilities (captions on videos). Ensure consistency: keep layouts uniform (the same "Save" button everywhere). Provide clear feedback: show action results ("Payment Successful" popup). Improve adaptability: responsive design (the website scales to mobile screens). Apply user-centred design (UCD): focus on real user goals and pilot-test. Use multimodal interaction: allow touch, voice or gesture inputs combined. Continuous testing: regularly update based on user feedback.

topics.title: 1.9 User Interface Design (UI vs UX)
topics.learn: UI design is the process of creating and organizing the visual elements of a software application so users can interact with it easily and efficiently. UX is the overall experience a user has while interacting with a system — how smooth, comfortable and satisfying it feels. UI is what you see; UX is how it feels.

topics.title: 1.9.3–1.9.5 Wireframing, Figma and Prototypes
topics.learn: 1.9.3 Wireframing is creating a basic visual outline or blueprint of a user interface before the final design. It plans the structure without focusing on colours or detailed graphics. Low-fidelity wireframes (Lo-Fi) A simple black-and-white sketch showing basic layout (boxes and lines). Used early to test and share ideas quickly. Focuses purely on structure and flow. High-fidelity prototypes (Hi-Fi) A detailed version that looks almost exactly like the final product. Includes real colours, fonts, images and interactive clickable buttons. Used for final user testing.

topics.title: 1.11 Test and Evaluate HCI (Evaluation Methods)
topics.learn: Testing checks if the product works properly (finding bugs). Evaluation determines whether it meets users' needs (usability). Together they improve the product before release. A school portal can be "bug-free" (testing passed) and still unusable if students cannot find the date sheet (evaluation failed). You need both.

topics.title: 1.11.2 Testing Methods (Usability, A/B, Automated)
topics.learn: Testing involves observing how the system behaves under specific conditions. Learn all seven methods. The three named in the heading — usability, A/B and automated — are the ones examiners ask most, but a complete answer also names the others. Usability testing: observing real users while they perform realistic tasks, to measure efficiency and satisfaction. If the user gets stuck, designers know where to fix the UI. Task-based testing: assigning a specific task (for example, "Find a product and add it to cart") and strictly measuring completion time, success rate and number of errors. Automated audits: software bots scan websites to detect technical issues such as broken links, slow loading speeds or low colour contrast. A/B testing: comparing two versions of an interface (A and B). Half the users see A, half see B. The one with more clicks or sign-ups wins. Compatibility testing: verifying the system on different browsers (Chrome, Safari), devices (mobiles, tablets, PCs) and operating systems. Performance and load testing: simulating high traffic (for example 10,000 users logging in at once) to see if speed drops or the server crashes. Keyboard and screen-reader walkthroughs: navigating using only the keyboard (Tab/Enter) or assistive technologies, to check accessibility for users with disabilities.

topics.title: 2.1 Analyze algorithms for correctness
topics.learn: An algorithm is correct if its output matches the expected results for a given input. Analysing correctness means showing that the algorithm produces the intended output for all valid inputs, not just one lucky example. Two methods are used in this course:

topics.title: 2.1.1 Trace Tables
topics.learn: A trace table is a technique used to monitor how the values of variables change during the execution of an algorithm. It is a paper execution of the code — a manual walkthrough, also called a dry run. You act as the computer and fill in one row after another. Purpose of trace tables Components of a trace table Dry running: execute the algorithm line by line by hand. Debugging: find logical errors where the algorithm runs but the output is wrong. Validation: check that the algorithm does what it is intended to do. Line / step number — which line is being executed. Variables — one column for every variable. Input / output — user inputs and printed results. Condition check — True/False for IF, WHILE, FOR, and similar tests.

topics.title: 2.1.2 Stepwise Reasoning
topics.learn: Stepwise reasoning (also called logic verification) breaks an algorithm into logical sections and checks the state of the algorithm at each stage. A state is a snapshot of what is true about the variables at that moment (for example, “Sum currently holds the total of the numbers seen so far”). You do not fill a row for every line. You think through the logic: Analyse each step of the algorithm. Check: does it start in a valid state? Does it handle all possible cases? Are the conditions correct? If the loop is correct at the start of an iteration, does it remain correct at the end?

topics.title: 2.2 Evaluating the Clarity of an Algorithm
topics.learn: Clarity means an algorithm is easy to read, understand and modify. In many cases, evaluating clarity is even more important than making the algorithm slightly faster. A clear algorithm is easier to maintain, debug and extend over time. The two key aspects of clarity are:
topics.urdu: وضاحت (Clarity) کا مطلب ہے الگورتھم پڑھنا، سمجھنا اور بدلنا آسان ہو۔ بہت سی صورتوں میں وضاحت رفتار سے بھی اہم ہے۔ اس کے دو حصے ہیں: ماڈیولریٹی (Modularity) یعنی کام کو حصوں میں بانٹنا، اور پڑھائی پن (Readability) یعنی متن اور بہاؤ صاف ہونا۔
